title.en: Similar figures and the Basic Proportionality Theorem

text.en: A photograph and its enlargement have the same shape but different sizes. Maps, models and shadows all work on the same idea: similarity.

Two figures with the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures. All congruent figures are similar, but similar figures need not be congruent.
Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
Now take triangle ABC and draw a line DE parallel to BC, meeting AB at D and AC at E.
The Basic Proportionality Theorem, also called Thales' theorem, says: AD by DB = AE by EC.
The converse is also true: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then it is parallel to the third side.
For example, if AD = 2 cm, DB = 3 cm and AE = 4 cm, then EC = 6 cm, because 2 by 3 = 4 by EC.
The proof uses triangles that share a height, so the ratio of their areas equals the ratio of their bases.
Never apply BPT unless you know that the line is parallel to one side.

problem.en: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, AD = 1.5 cm, DB = 3 cm and AE = 1 cm. Find EC.

prompt.en: State and use the Basic Proportionality Theorem.

requiredIdeas.en: Divides the other two sides in the same ratio

points.en: Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional sides.
BPT: a line parallel to a side divides the other two sides in the same ratio.
Converse: dividing in the same ratio implies parallel.
